title: Montreal students reeling from police violence at Nov. 13 education austerity protest
summary: Montreal students are denouncing the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) for what they call unjustified acts of violence during a protest against education austerity that took place on…

image.caption: None of the protesters CBC News interviewed said they were told to leave the site of the Nov. 13 student protest before Montreal police deployed tear gas. (Khaled Yeddes/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal students are denouncing the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) for what they call unjustified acts of violence during a protest against education austerity that took place on Friday.

The Nov. 13 protest was organized by the Coalition de résistance pour l'unité étudiante syndicale (CRUES), which called on the province to reform its student financial assistance program and increase funding for CEGEPs and universities.

While protesters in attendance described the mood in Victoria Square, where they first gathered, as originally festive and joyous, there was a shift as the group of roughly 200 people began their procession into the streets.

An SPVM spokesperson said that a demonstrator started to commit mischief, breaking a window and damaging a vehicle, which led to the protest being declared illegal. According to police, a firework was also fired at an officer by that one demonstrator.
"We had to deploy tear gas to spread the crowd that was aggressive at that time," said Raphaël Bergeron.

Police say two people were arrested for armed assault on a police officer and another was arrested for assault on a police officer. Police noted eight incidents of mischief involving buildings or vehicles, but no citizen injuries.
'It made me feel a bit of despair for humanity'
Maxim Lepage, a 20-year-old psychoeducation student at the Université de Montréal, remembers the events of the protest differently.
She said she received no verbal warning from police to disperse, and only knew something had gone wrong after tear gas starting hitting the crowd.

She said that the people she was protesting with ran into a side street to flee from an advancing group of roughly 30 officers. Lepage was running away on St-Dominique Street when she turned around, and says she saw a man alone on the ground, surrounded by officers who were kicking him.

items: Montreal police use tear gas to disperse downtown student protest

blocks.text: Lepage said that when she and her friend turned around to address the officers, her friend was hit in the throat with a police riot shield. Lepage then said she was hit in the face with another officer's shield, causing her nose to begin bleeding.
Maxim Lepage says she was hit in the face by a police officer's riot shield during the Nov. 13 student protest. (Submitted by Maxim Lepage)

It turned out to be broken. Lepage was given first-aid support by paramedics at the protest, before going to the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) in a taxi, and waiting for 15 hours to be treated. A friend of Lepage's suspected she might have a concussion, and also waited there for eight hours, before ultimately leaving untreated.

Lepage waited 15 hours in the emergency room at the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) with a broken nose. There, she saw three other injured protesters from the Nov. 13 demonstration. (Submitted by Maxim Lepage)
Lepage says she also saw two other protesters at the hospital waiting for medical attention: one who had hurt their leg, and another who had received a projectile to the face.
Urgences-santé said that three people from the protest were transported by ambulance to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and that one person refused transport.
"It was pretty shocking to see a group from the protest in the emergency room," said Lepage. "It made me feel a bit of despair for humanity."
'Easily the most terrifying seconds of my life'

Mere feet away from Lepage in the emergency room was Rebecca Mota, an 18-year-old CEGEP student from Collège de Maisonneuve. She was the protester with the injured leg, needing X-rays for a potential fracture, and getting referred to another doctor for tenderness in her abdomen.

A member of her school's student association, Mota had encouraged a number of friends, who had not participated in any protests before, to attend the demonstration with her. She had been expecting it to go peacefully.
"No one was prepared for the way it was going to go," said Mota. "They threw so much gas in such little time."

Like Lepage, Mota also recalled the tear gas coming without warning. Mota and her friends began to run away, but kept being caught up to by police. Eventually, amid the chaos, she fell to the ground and couldn't get back up.
"The police pushed someone, and that person fell on me," said Mota. "Despite the fact that we were still on the floor and that we couldn't get up, the police would still push us with their shields."
"It was horrible, the time I spent on the floor was easily the most terrifying seconds of my life."
Then, Mota remembered not being able to leave, despite wanting to, because the protesters were surrounded by officers.
Both she and Lepage had come to the protest initially to draw attention to the circumstances of austerity facing their education system.

blocks.text: Mota says knows fellow students who work 20-hour weeks while studying for another 30 in class, not including time spent on homework. She says that they live in economic precarity, and that the support their schools offer is lacking.
Lepage, for her part, says she has worked over 400 unpaid hours for her university internship, on top of holding down a job and studying, and that she has regularly skipped meals to get by.
For her, the protest was to show that youth have a voice, to exercise her democratic rights, and to get the attention of the provincial government.
Instead, she said, "it just showed at what point the government was badly doing its job."

"I was really hoping that the protest would be a way for students from so many schools to get together and show that we all care about this issue," said Mota. "For so many people, it was their first experience [at a protest], and they got attacked."
Police repression historically harder on students, say advocates

Laurence Guénette, the co-ordinator and spokesperson for the Ligue des droits et libertés (LDL), said that her organization has received several photos documenting injuries students received at the protest at the hands of the police.

"The testimonies we have really question the narrative of clashes taking place between the demonstrators and the police," said Guénette. "It's more like the brutality of the police repression is absolutely unacceptable."
She said multiple people who ran away from the police during the dispersal operation were "strongly hit."

While shocked, she said that the LDL is not surprised, given the police have historically been harder on students during other periods of protest against educational conditions, namely strikes against tuition raises in 2012.
Karine Cliche, a professor from CEGEP Montmorency who was present on Friday, also participated in student protests during the 2012 strikes.
"This protest, it's the first time I saw a repression that was so fast to stop a peaceful movement and a legitimate cause of protest," she said.
The protest took place on Friday and began at around 2 p.m. Square-Victoria in downtown Montreal. (Philippe Robitaille-Grou/Radio-Canada)
Cliche says police pepper sprayed her multiple times while she was at the front lines of the protest.
Québec Solidaire MNA Gisèle Pouhe Njall showed up to the protest to show her support for students. She witnessed a young man being beaten by officers after falling down of his own accord.
"He didn't mean any wrong, he just happened to fall," she said. "He tried to step back up, and I saw with my own eyes police officers going to him and beating him."

blocks.text: Pouhe Njall said she was also afraid when people next to her were hit by police with shields.
None of the protesters CBC News interviewed said that they heard a verbal notice to leave the protest before tear gas was deployed.
The SPVM and the mayor's office did not respond in time for publication to a request for comment on the allegations of abuse made by protesters against officers during the dispersal operation.
'We stopped talking about the students' demands'

Following the protest, Elsie Lefebvre, the minister of higher education, and Guy Lapointe Jr., the domestic security minister, posted the same message on X, stating that the government recognizes students' right to protest, but that they condemned acts of violence and vandalism from protesters during the demonstration that put those peacefully gathering at risk.
Pouhe Njall called on Lefebvre to meet with students to address their concerns directly.

"What I absolutely find scary is that we stopped talking about the students' demands," she said. "The cost of living is so high that our students in Quebec cannot go to school, have an internship, study at the same time, eat and have a full belly and a roof over their heads."
"Unfortunately, we've lost track of that, with what happened yesterday."
The student mobilization could continue into the winter semester, with student associations expected to vote later this month on whether to call an unlimited general strike.
For their part, Lepage and Mota said that Friday's events did not dim their desire to have their voices heard.
"It makes me want to protest more," said Lepage.
Montreal city councillors trade barbs
Jim Beis, the Montreal executive committee member responsible for public security, defended the police intervention during a city council meeting question period.
He said officers did what was necessary to protect both the general public and the demonstrators.

"The images we all saw on social media show a portion of this interaction, but the only thing I can tell you is that I know the teams are trained to intervene in these cases, and that is exactly what they did," he said.

He was responding to questions from Projet Montréal Coun. Marie Plourde, who said citizens have a right to be worried when they see riot police deployed against student demonstrators. She asked if the city plans to follow New York City's lead in reforming crowd-control tactics to ensure protests remain safe.
